author: NewsBreak
title: Watch Your Head: Cold snap could send Florida Iguanas tumbling from trees, says official - NewsBreak
text:
7 hours ago Photo by Roberto Sotelo on Unsplash That chill in the air means more than just pulling out your jacket. It might mean dodging falling iguanas.
As temperatures plunge across Florida this week, wildlife officials are warning residents about an unusual hazard: lizards literally dropping from the sky. When Florida's thermometer dips near freezing, green iguanas go into something called "cold-stunning." Their bodies essentially hit the pause button.
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission posted a reminder earlier this week as cooler weather swept through the Sunshine State. These nonnative lizards lose all muscle control when temperatures drop that low.
Think of it like their batteries dying. Iguanas need sun to keep their body temperature regulated. Without it, they can't hold onto tree branches.
They just fall.
"I don't like going outside in my backyard when the temperature falls," one resident shared this morning, while walking their dogs. "I see these almost lifeless Iguanas fall out of the trees, and they not only scare me, but frighten the dogs."
What's Happening
After dipping into the mid 40 degrees on New Year's Eve, temperatures are anticipated to drop even lower and even into the 20s and 30s across portions of Florida. That's cold enough to completely immobilize these tropical creatures.
The lizards start losing their grip around 50 degrees. Below that, they're basically frozen in place . Here's the catch: they're usually not dead. After a few hours, most snap out of it.
If you spot a stunned iguana on the ground, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has clear advice: leave it alone.
Don't bring it inside your house or car. These lizards recover fast, sometimes faster than you'd expect. A confused iguana can bite, scratch, or whip you with its tail.
Keep your pets away, too. And remember, relocating them is illegal without a permit.
Iguanas have lived in South Florida since the 1960s. They've caused serious damage to seawalls and sidewalks over the years. Florida added them to its prohibited species list in April 2021 .
Property owners can remove them humanely, but these tropical lizards aren't protected by wildlife laws.
